title: He Was Born in Melbourne to a Tamil Father and an Anglo-Indian Mother. In Vancouver, Nishan Velupillay Became the First Indian-Origin Player at a World Cup in 20 Years.
excerpt: Four players with Indian roots are scattered across the FIFA World Cup 2026 — from Punjab to Kerala to Sri Lankan Tamil heritage. None wear the India jersey. All carry the diaspora story.
body:
When Australia's Tony Popovic sent Nishan Velupillay onto the pitch in the 61st minute at BC Place in Vancouver on Saturday night, the substitution barely registered in the global match commentary. Australia were already leading Türkiye 1-0 in Group D. The Socceroos were protecting a lead. Another winger, in, to keep fresh legs on the flanks.

But for an entire diaspora watching from continents away, the moment carried a weight that had nothing to do with tactical adjustments.

Velupillay, a 25-year-old Melbourne Victory forward, became the first player of Indian origin to appear at a FIFA World Cup since France's Vikash Dhorasoo took the field in Germany in 2006. Twenty years. That is how long the gap lasted.

## A Melbourne Story with Tamil and Anglo-Indian Roots

Velupillay was born and raised in Melbourne's southeastern suburbs. His father, Sasinath, is of Sri Lankan Tamil descent with Malaysian roots. His mother, Gillian, is Anglo-Indian. He attended Mazenod College in Mulgrave, started playing at Glen Eira FC, and worked his way through the Melbourne Victory academy — the classic Australian grassroots-to-professional pathway, except his family story traces back through Jaffna, Kuala Lumpur, and the subcontinent.

He made his international debut in October 2024 during a World Cup qualifier against China, coming off the bench in the 83rd minute and scoring within seven minutes. Since then, he has earned seven caps and three goals — every one of them in a qualifier. His inclusion in Australia's 26-man World Cup squad was a reward for consistency, not a gesture.

Australia won the match 2-0. Velupillay played his role, holding shape as the Socceroos closed out the result. But his appearance was the headline across Indian sports pages by morning.



> **"He grew up in a "very typical Punjabi family with a lot of uncles and aunties and cousins," as he told *Sportstar* — backyard cricket, a bit of basketball, and the family grocery store."**


## Sarpreet Singh: From a Jalandhar Family to FC Bayern Munich

Velupillay is not the only Indian connection at this World Cup. On Monday, when New Zealand face Iran in California, Sarpreet Singh will almost certainly become the second Indian-origin player to take the field at the 2026 tournament.

Singh's story is arguably the more remarkable one. Born in Auckland to Punjabi parents whose family originates from Jalandhar, he was enrolled at the Wynton Rufer Soccer Academy at age seven by his mother, Sarabjit. He grew up in a "very typical Punjabi family with a lot of uncles and aunties and cousins," as he told *Sportstar* — backyard cricket, a bit of basketball, and the family grocery store.

From there, the path took him to Wellington Phoenix, then to FC Bayern Munich, where he became the first player of Indian heritage to represent the German giants. Injuries and loan spells across Germany, Portugal, and Serbia followed before he returned to Wellington Phoenix in 2026 to rebuild his fitness for the World Cup.

"I don't say it's added pressure," Singh said in an interview with *Livemint* from Miami. "I just want to do my best to lift the names of Indian people, and there is no better stage to do it than the World Cup."

He scored his first international goal against Kenya at the Intercontinental Cup — in Mumbai. "That was a crazy experience," he recalled. "It's a little bit strange being a Singh and playing for New Zealand in India against India."

## Tahsin Mohammed Jamshid: Kerala's First Son at the World Cup

Then there is the youngest of the group. Tahsin Mohammed Jamshid is 19 years old, born in Doha to Malayali parents from Kannur, Kerala. His father, Jamshid, played football for the University of Calicut before moving to Qatar in 1996. His mother is Shaima. Tahsin trained at Qatar's Aspire Academy before joining Al Duhail, where he emerged as one of the country's most promising young attackers.

Qatar have already played at this World Cup — their dramatic 94th-minute equaliser against Switzerland in a 1-1 draw was one of the tournament's first great moments. Whether Jamshid featured or will feature in remaining group matches, his selection alone prompted a rare moment of football pride in Kerala.

Shashi Tharoor, the veteran Indian parliamentarian and Thiruvananthapuram MP, wrote on X: "Kerala has always loved football with an ardour bordering on devotion, yet for all our passion we had never sent one of our own to the sport's grandest stage — until now."

## Samuel Moutoussamy: The Tamil Thread Through Paris and Congo

The fourth Indian connection is the most distant and the most fascinating. Samuel Moutoussamy, a 29-year-old defensive midfielder, represents DR Congo. He was born in Paris to a Congolese mother and an Indo-Guadeloupean father — his father's family traces back to the Tamil community through the Indian diaspora in the French Caribbean.

Moutoussamy has 57 caps for Congo and spent much of his club career with Nantes in Ligue 1 before moving to the Netherlands, Turkey, and currently Greek side Atromitos. DR Congo face Portugal on June 17 in Houston, and Moutoussamy is expected to anchor the midfield.

## The Bittersweet Truth

India qualified for the 1950 FIFA World Cup but withdrew, citing travel costs and a preference for the 1952 Olympics. Seventy-six years later, the national team still has not appeared at football's grandest tournament. The expanded 48-team format was supposed to open the door; it did not.

But in Vancouver, Auckland, Doha, and Paris, four families with roots in Tamil Nadu, Punjab, Kerala, and the French Caribbean carried the Indian story onto the pitch anyway. None of them wore blue. All of them wore something harder to see and impossible to miss.
